title: Abbreviations and Math Review
description: Exam 4 review, matched to the professor's Exam 4 study guide: the class's common abbreviations, unit conversions, and intake in mL, including ice chips, with the rounding and zero rules. The numbers change on every attempt.

questions.stem: A client has a new prescription: “Metoprolol 25 mg PO bid.” Which instruction should the nurse give the client?
options: “Take one dose by mouth three times a day.”
“Take one dose by mouth on alternate days.”
“Let one dose dissolve under your tongue twice a day.”
“Take one dose by mouth twice a day.”
questions.rationale:
PO means by mouth, and bid means twice a day.

Three times a day isn't the right answer: that's tid, and four times a day is qid. Alternate days aren't what bid means, and dissolving a dose under the tongue is a different route (sublingual), not PO.

Takeaway: bid = twice a day, tid = three times, qid = four times; PO = by mouth.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for surgery tomorrow morning, and the order reads “NPO after midnight.” Which instruction should the nurse give the client?
options: “After midnight, you may have ice chips, but no food.”
“After midnight, you may have water, but no food.”
“Don't eat or drink anything after midnight.”
“After midnight, you may have clear liquids, like broth and juice.”
questions.rationale:
NPO means nothing by mouth: no food or fluids, starting at the time in the order.

Ice chips aren't the right answer: they melt into water, which is a fluid taken by mouth. Water and clear liquids are fluids too, and an exception would need the provider's order.

Takeaway: NPO = nothing by mouth: no food, no fluids, no ice chips, unless the provider orders otherwise.

questions.stem: At the start of a shift, a nurse finds four new medication orders for a client. Which order should the nurse carry out first?
options: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO q6h PRN pain
questions.rationale:
STAT means immediately, so that order comes first.

The acetaminophen isn't the right answer: PRN means as needed, so it's given when the client has pain, and the client hasn't reported any. bid (twice a day) and qam (every morning) are scheduled doses that follow the unit's schedule.

Takeaway: STAT = now; PRN = as needed; scheduled doses (bid, qam) follow the schedule.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's medication orders. For each order, click to specify when the nurse should give the medication.
rows: Ondansetron 4 mg PO q8h PRN nausea
questions.rationale:
ac means before meals and pc after meals (a for before, p for after). qam is every morning, qpm every evening, and PRN as needed. In “q8h PRN,” PRN means the dose is given only when needed, and q8h sets the shortest time between doses.

Putting the ondansetron on a schedule of every 8 hours is a mistake: PRN means it's given only for nausea, no more often than every 8 hours.

Takeaway: ac before meals, pc after meals, qam every morning, qpm every evening, PRN as needed.

questions.stem: On admission, a client says, “I'm not allergic to any medicines, but I break out in hives when I eat peanuts.” Which entry should the nurse document?
questions.rationale:
NKDA means no known drug allergies, which fits this client, and the peanut allergy is recorded too, with the reaction.

NKA isn't the right answer: it means no known allergies of any kind, and this client has a food allergy. Leaving out the peanut allergy hides a real risk, and peanuts aren't a drug.

Takeaway: NKDA = no known drug allergies; NKA = no known allergies at all. Record every allergy and its reaction.

questions.stem: A prescription reads “Acetaminophen 650 mg PO x1 for headache.” Six hours after the dose, the client's headache returns. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give another dose, since 6 hours have passed
Give another dose, since the order lists it for headache
Contact the provider for a new order
Wait 2 more hours, then give another dose
questions.rationale:
x1 means one time. The order was for a single dose, so it's complete, and another dose needs a new order.

Giving another dose since 6 hours have passed isn't the right answer: that would fit an order like “q6h PRN,” but this order gives no frequency. The headache is the reason for the dose, not permission to repeat it.

Takeaway: x1 = one time; a repeat dose needs a new order.

questions.stem: A prescription reads “Timolol eye drops, 1 drop OU bid.” How should the nurse give this medication?
options: One drop in each eye, three times a day
One drop in each eye, twice a day
One drop in the left eye, twice a day
One drop in each ear, twice a day
questions.rationale:
OU means both eyes, and bid means twice a day.

The left eye isn't the right answer: that's OS, and the right eye is OD. Three times a day is tid, and the ears have their own abbreviations, which are easy to mix up with the eyes'.

Takeaway: OD right eye, OS left eye, OU both eyes.

questions.stem: A client's orders include “I&O” and “Fluids ad lib.” Which action should the nurse take?
options: Limit fluids to a set amount, and measure all intake and output
Let the client drink freely, and measure all intake and output
Let the client drink freely, and measure only the IV fluids
Offer fluids only at meals, and measure all intake and output
questions.rationale:
Ad lib means as much as desired, so the client may drink freely, and I&O means intake and output, so every amount in and out is measured and recorded.

Limiting fluids isn't the right answer: a fluid restriction needs its own order, and ad lib means the opposite. I&O covers everything taken in and put out, not just IV fluids, and meals aren't the only time to drink.

Takeaway: ad lib = as desired; I&O = measure and record intake and output.

questions.stem: A nurse reads this entry in a client's record: “A&O x3. RLE edema. Lungs WNL.” Which statement in the hand-off report is accurate?
options: “The client is alert and oriented, with swelling in the right arm.”
“The client is alert and oriented, with swelling in the left leg.”
“The client is alert and oriented, with swelling in the right leg.”
“The client is alert and oriented, with abnormal lung sounds.”
questions.rationale:
A&O x3 means alert and oriented to person, place, and time; RLE is the right lower extremity, the right leg; and WNL means within normal limits.

The right arm isn't the right answer: that's RUE, the right upper extremity. The left leg is LLE, and WNL means the lungs are normal.

Takeaway: RUE right arm, LUE left arm, RLE right leg, LLE left leg.

questions.stem: A nurse is checking a classmate's answers on a medication math worksheet. Which answers are written correctly?
questions.rationale:
Two rules apply: no trailing zero after a decimal point, and a leading zero before a decimal point for any amount less than 1. 0.75 mL, 20 mg, and 0.33 mg follow both.

1.50 g isn't written correctly: the trailing zero should go (1.5 g). 2.0 mL has a trailing zero too (2 mL), and .5 mg needs its leading zero (0.5 mg). A missed decimal point turns 2.0 into 20 and .5 into 5, a 10-fold error.

Takeaway: No trailing zeros, and a leading zero before every decimal point.

questions.stem: A nurse calculates that a client's dose is {v} mL. How should the nurse write the amount to give?
questions.rationale:
The class's rule: an amount less than 1 mL is rounded to the hundredth, with a leading zero. {v} rounds to {=round(v, 2)} mL.

{=round(v, 1)} mL isn't the right answer: rounding to the tenth is the rule for amounts over 1 mL. .{=round(v * 100)} mL leaves out the leading zero, and {v} mL isn't rounded at all.

Takeaway: Under 1 mL: round to the hundredth, with a leading zero.

questions.stem: A nurse's calculation for an oral liquid comes to {v} mL. Which amount should the nurse prepare?
questions.rationale:
The class's rule: an amount over 1 mL is rounded to the tenth. {v} rounds to {=round(v, 1)} mL.

{=floor(v * 10) / 10} mL isn't the right answer: it drops the hundredths instead of rounding, and a hundredths digit of 5 or more rounds up. {v} mL isn't rounded, and {=round(v)} mL rounds too far, to a whole number.

Takeaway: Over 1 mL: round to the tenth; 5 or more rounds up.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed {g} g of an antibiotic. How many milligrams should the nurse prepare?
questions.rationale:
1 g = 1,000 mg, and a gram is the larger unit, so multiply: {g} × 1,000 = {answer} mg.

Dividing by 1,000 is a mistake: changing to a smaller unit gives a bigger number.

Takeaway: g to mg: × 1,000.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed {mg} mg of a medication. How many grams is this dose?
questions.rationale:
1,000 mg = 1 g, so divide: {mg} ÷ 1,000 = {answer} g. An answer under 1 needs a leading zero, and one like 1.5 is written without a trailing zero.

Multiplying by 1,000 is a mistake: a gram is the larger unit, so the number of grams is smaller.

Takeaway: mg to g: ÷ 1,000.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed {mcg} mcg of a medication. How many milligrams is this dose?
questions.rationale:
1,000 mcg = 1 mg, so divide: {mcg} ÷ 1,000 = {answer} mg, with a leading zero.

Multiplying is a mistake: micrograms are the smaller unit, so the number of milligrams is smaller.

Takeaway: mcg to mg: ÷ 1,000.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed {mg} mg of a medication. How many micrograms is this dose?
questions.rationale:
1 mg = 1,000 mcg, so multiply: {mg} × 1,000 = {answer} mcg.

Dividing is a mistake: micrograms are smaller, so there are more of them.

Takeaway: mg to mcg: × 1,000.

questions.stem: A newborn weighed {b} g at birth and has lost {loss} g by day 2. What is the newborn's weight on day 2 in kilograms?
questions.rationale:
Subtract first: {b} − {loss} = {=b - loss} g. Then 1,000 g = 1 kg, so divide: {=b - loss} ÷ 1,000 = {answer} kg.

Converting the birth weight alone is a mistake: the question asks for today's weight.

Takeaway: g to kg: ÷ 1,000; subtract in one unit first.

questions.stem: A client's total intake for the day is {ml} mL. How many liters is this?
questions.rationale:
1,000 mL = 1 L, so divide: {ml} ÷ 1,000 = {answer} L. Whole numbers and tenths are written without trailing zeros (2, not 2.00; 1.5, not 1.50).

Multiplying is a mistake: liters are the larger unit, so the number of liters is smaller.

Takeaway: mL to L: ÷ 1,000.

questions.stem: A client weighs {lb} lb. How many kilograms does the client weigh?
questions.rationale:
1 kg = 2.2 lb, so divide by 2.2: {lb} ÷ 2.2 = {=round(lb / 2.2, 2)}, which rounds to {answer} kg.

Multiplying by 2.2 is a mistake: it gives a number bigger than the pounds, and a weight in kilograms is the smaller number.

Takeaway: lb to kg: ÷ 2.2.

questions.stem: A child weighs {kg} kg. How many pounds does the child weigh?
questions.rationale:
1 kg = 2.2 lb, so multiply: {kg} × 2.2 = {answer} lb. A whole number is written without a trailing zero.

Dividing by 2.2 is a mistake: pounds are the smaller unit, so there are more of them.

Takeaway: kg to lb: × 2.2.

questions.stem: A client is to take {t} tsp of a liquid medication. How many milliliters is this dose?
questions.rationale:
1 tsp = 5 mL: {t} × 5 = {answer} mL.

Using 15 mL is a mistake: that's a tablespoon.

Takeaway: 1 tsp = 5 mL; 1 tbsp = 15 mL.

questions.stem: A client's temperature is {c} °C. What is this temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?
questions.rationale:
°F = °C × 9/5 + 32. First multiply: {c} × 9/5 = {=round(c * 9 / 5, 2)}. Then add 32: {=round(c * 9 / 5 + 32, 2)}, which rounds to {answer} °F. A whole-number answer is written without a trailing zero.

Adding 32 before multiplying is a mistake: multiply first, then add.

Takeaway: °F = °C × 9/5 + 32.

questions.stem: An IV medication is to infuse over {m} minutes. How many hours is this?
questions.rationale:
60 minutes = 1 hour, so divide: {m} ÷ 60 = {=round(m / 60, 4)}, which rounds to {answer} hours, with a leading zero for an answer under 1.

Dividing by 100 is a mistake: an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.

Takeaway: Minutes to hours: ÷ 60.

questions.stem: A client drank {part} of a can of ginger ale that holds {oz} oz. How many milliliters should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
{oz} oz × 30 = {=oz * 30} mL in the can, and the client drank {part} of it: {answer} mL.

Recording the whole can is a mistake: intake is what the client actually drank.

Takeaway: 1 oz = 30 mL; record only what was taken in.

questions.stem: At breakfast, a client drank {a} oz of orange juice and {b} of coffee, and had {c} mL of broth. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Juice: {a} × 30 = {=a * 30} mL. Coffee: {b} × 240 = {=b * 240} mL (1 cup = 8 oz = 240 mL). Broth: {c} mL. Total: {answer} mL.

Counting a cup as 30 mL is a mistake: 30 mL is one ounce, and a cup is 8 ounces.

Takeaway: 1 cup = 8 oz = 240 mL.

questions.stem: A client on a fluid restriction of {lim} mL a day has had {a} oz of juice and {b} of tea so far. How many more milliliters may the client have today?
questions.rationale:
Intake so far: juice {a} × 30 = {=a * 30} mL and tea {b} × 240 = {=b * 240} mL, for {=a * 30 + b * 240} mL. Left for today: {lim} − {=a * 30 + b * 240} = {answer} mL.

Subtracting the ounces and cups before converting them is a mistake: change everything to mL first.

Takeaway: Convert to mL, add up the intake, then subtract it from the limit.

questions.stem: A client's goal is to drink {l} L of fluid today. So far, the client has had {ml} mL. How many more milliliters does the client need?
questions.rationale:
{l} L = {=l * 1000} mL, and {=l * 1000} − {ml} = {answer} mL.

Subtracting before converting the liters is a mistake: change to the same unit first.

Takeaway: Convert to the same unit before you subtract.

questions.stem: A client drank {part} of a bottle of water that holds {oz} oz. Which amount should the nurse record as intake?
questions.rationale:
{oz} oz × 30 = {=oz * 30} mL in the bottle, and {part} of it is {=oz * 30 * part} mL.

{=oz * 30 * (1 - part)} mL isn't the right answer: that's what's left in the bottle, not what the client drank. {=oz * 30} mL is the whole bottle, and {=oz * 15 * part} mL uses 15 mL for each ounce, which is a tablespoon.

Takeaway: Intake is the amount the client drank, with 1 oz = 30 mL.

questions.stem: A client took {t} tablespoons of a liquid supplement and drank {oz} oz of milk. How many milliliters should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Supplement: {t} × 15 = {=t * 15} mL. Milk: {oz} × 30 = {=oz * 30} mL. Total: {answer} mL.

Using 5 mL for each tablespoon is a mistake: 5 mL is a teaspoon.

Takeaway: 1 tbsp = 15 mL; 1 oz = 30 mL.

questions.stem: Over a shift, a client drank {a} oz of water and {b} oz of juice, ate {c} mL of soup, and vomited {v} mL. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Intake only: water {a} × 30 = {=a * 30} mL, juice {b} × 30 = {=b * 30} mL, and soup {c} mL, for {answer} mL. The {v} mL of vomit is output, recorded on its own.

Subtracting the vomit from the intake is a mistake: intake and output are separate totals.

Takeaway: Record intake and output separately; never subtract one from the other.

questions.stem: On a lunch tray, a client has a carton holding {m} oz of milk and a bowl with {s} mL of soup. The client drinks all the milk and eats {part} of the soup. How many milliliters should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Milk: {m} × 30 = {=m * 30} mL, all of it. Soup: {part} of {s} mL = {=s * part} mL. Total: {answer} mL.

Recording the whole bowl of soup is a mistake: count only the part the client ate.

Takeaway: Convert each item, count what was actually taken, then add.

questions.stem: A client ate {c} mL of ice chips. How many milliliters of fluid intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Ice chips melt down to about half their volume in water, so the nurse records half: {c} ÷ 2 = {answer} mL.

Recording the full {c} mL is a mistake: the ice takes up about twice the space the water will.

Takeaway: Ice chips: record half the volume.

questions.stem: A client in labor had {n} of ice chips this shift. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record? (1 cup = 240 mL)
questions.rationale:
{n} × 240 = {=n * 240} mL of ice chips, and ice chips count as half: {=n * 240} ÷ 2 = {answer} mL.

Counting the cups at their full volume is a mistake: convert to mL, then halve the ice chips.

Takeaway: Convert to mL first, then halve the ice chips.

questions.stem: A client ate {a} oz of ice chips and drank {b} oz of water. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Ice chips: {a} × 30 = {=a * 30} mL, and half of that is {=a * 15} mL. Water: {b} × 30 = {=b * 30} mL. Total: {answer} mL.

Halving the water too is a mistake: only the ice chips are halved.

Takeaway: Halve the ice chips, not the other fluids.

questions.stem: After surgery, a client had {c} mL of ice chips, {j} oz of apple juice, and {b} mL of broth. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Ice chips: {c} ÷ 2 = {=c / 2} mL. Juice: {j} × 30 = {=j * 30} mL. Broth: {b} mL. Total: {answer} mL.

Adding the ice chips at their full volume is a mistake: they count as half.

Takeaway: List each item in mL, halve the ice chips, then add.

questions.stem: A client ate {part} of a cup of ice chips that holds {cup} mL. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
The client ate {part} of {cup} mL = {=cup * part} mL of ice chips, and ice chips count as half: {answer} mL.

Halving only once is the key: take the part eaten, then halve it for ice. Halving the cup and skipping the part eaten is a mistake.

Takeaway: Part eaten first, then half for ice chips.

questions.stem: A client's intake for the shift was {c} mL of ice chips and {w} mL of water. Which total should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Ice chips count as half: {c} ÷ 2 = {=c / 2} mL. Water counts in full: {w} mL. Total: {=c / 2 + w} mL.

{=(c + w) / 2} mL isn't the right answer: it halves the water too. {=c + w} mL counts the ice chips at full volume, and {=c / 2} mL leaves out the water.

Takeaway: Halve the ice chips only, then add the other fluids.

questions.stem: A client on a fluid restriction of {lim} mL a day has had {w} oz of water and {c} mL of ice chips so far. How many more milliliters may the client have today?
questions.rationale:
So far: water {w} × 30 = {=w * 30} mL, and ice chips {c} ÷ 2 = {=c / 2} mL, for {=w * 30 + c / 2} mL. Left for today: {lim} − {=w * 30 + c / 2} = {answer} mL.

Counting the ice chips at full volume is a mistake: it would cut the client's remaining fluids by more than it should.

Takeaway: Ice chips count as half toward a fluid restriction too.

questions.stem: A client ate {c} mL of ice chips and drank {j} oz of ginger ale, then vomited {v} mL. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Intake only: ice chips {c} ÷ 2 = {=c / 2} mL and ginger ale {j} × 30 = {=j * 30} mL, for {answer} mL. The {v} mL of vomit is output, recorded on its own.

Subtracting the vomit from the intake is a mistake: intake and output are separate totals.

Takeaway: Halve the ice chips; record output separately.

questions.stem: A nurse is recording a client's intake. Why does the nurse record ice chips as half of their measured volume?
options: About half of the ice chips melt before the client eats them
Ice chips melt down to about half as much water
Half of the water from ice chips leaves the body as output
The body absorbs just half of the water in ice chips
questions.rationale:
Ice is mostly air spaces between the chips, so a cup of ice chips melts down to about half a cup of water. The nurse records the water the client actually took in.

Melting before the client eats them isn't the right answer: the half counts because of the space between the chips, not because of melting in the cup. Output and absorption have nothing to do with how intake is recorded.

Takeaway: Ice chips = half their volume in water.

questions.stem: Over 8 hours, a client ate {c1} mL of ice chips in the morning and {c2} mL in the afternoon, and drank {t} of tea. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record? (1 cup = 240 mL)
questions.rationale:
Ice chips: {c1} + {c2} = {=c1 + c2} mL, halved = {=(c1 + c2) / 2} mL. Tea: {t} × 240 = {=t * 240} mL. Total: {answer} mL.

Halving only one of the two servings of ice chips is a mistake: every serving of ice chips counts as half.

Takeaway: Add all the ice chips, halve them, then add the other fluids.

questions.stem: A client has a prescription for “Acetaminophen 650 mg PO q6h PRN pain.” The client's last dose was at 0800. At 1300, the client asks for another dose. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give half of the dose now and the other half at 1400, as the client prefers
Explain that acetaminophen can't be given again until tomorrow morning
Give the dose now, since PRN means the client can have it when asked
Explain that the next dose can be given at 1400, and offer comfort measures
questions.rationale:
q6h PRN means as needed, but no more often than every 6 hours. The last dose was at 0800, so the next one can be given at 1400; until then, the nurse offers other comfort measures, like repositioning or ice.

Giving it now isn't right: PRN lets the client decide whether to take a dose, not how often. Half now and half at 1400 changes the prescribed dose, which the nurse can't do. Not until tomorrow isn't right: q6h allows up to four doses a day.

Takeaway: PRN: when needed. q6h: at least 6 hours apart. Together: only when needed, and no sooner than 6 hours.

questions.stem: A client has a prescription for “Ondansetron 4 mg PO q8h x3 doses.” The nurse gave the first dose at 0600. When should the nurse give the last dose?
options: On a q8h schedule until the nausea stops
questions.rationale:
q8h means every 8 hours, and x3 doses means three doses in all: 0600, 1400, and 2200.

1400 isn't right: it's the second dose. 0600 the next day counts three doses after the first one, which makes four. Until the nausea stops ignores the x3, which ends the order after the third dose.

Takeaway: x3 means three times in all, counting the first.

questions.stem: A client has a prescription for “Latanoprost 1 drop OS hs.” How should the nurse give this medication?
options: One drop in the right eye at bedtime
One drop in both eyes at bedtime
One drop in the left eye each hour
One drop in the left eye at bedtime
questions.rationale:
OS is the left eye, and hs is the hour of sleep, bedtime: one drop in the left eye at bedtime.

The right eye is OD, and both eyes are OU. Each hour mixes up hs with h, which means hour, as in q1h.

Takeaway: OD right eye, OS left eye, OU both eyes; hs at bedtime.

questions.stem: A client has a prescription for “Docusate 100 mg PO tid pc.” Which schedule should the nurse follow?
options: Three times a day, after meals
Four times a day, after meals and at bedtime
Three times a day, before meals
questions.rationale:
tid is three times a day, and pc is after meals (p for post): three times a day, after meals.

Before meals is ac. Twice a day is bid, and four times a day is qid.

Takeaway: bid 2, tid 3, qid 4 times a day; ac before meals, pc after.

questions.stem: A client's allergy band reads “ASA.” Which medication order should the nurse question?
options: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO q6h PRN pain
questions.rationale:
ASA is aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid), so the aspirin order needs to be questioned before any dose is given.

Acetaminophen isn't right: its abbreviation is APA, a different drug, and the two are easy to mix up. Docusate and famotidine aren't related to aspirin.

Takeaway: ASA aspirin, APA acetaminophen, PCN penicillin: read allergy abbreviations letter by letter.

questions.stem: A client has a DNR order. The client's temperature rises to 101.8°F, and the provider prescribes acetaminophen. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Ask the provider to cancel the DNR order before giving it
Give the acetaminophen if the family agrees to it
Hold the acetaminophen, since a DNR order means no treatment
questions.rationale:
DNR means do not resuscitate: no CPR if the heart or breathing stops. Every other treatment goes on, so the nurse gives the acetaminophen as prescribed.

Holding it isn't right: a DNR order isn't an order to stop care. Canceling the DNR isn't needed, since the order doesn't affect this treatment, and the family's agreement isn't needed for a prescribed medication.

Takeaway: DNR: no CPR. Care, comfort, and treatment continue.

questions.stem: Before a client's surgery, a nurse checks that the H&P is on the chart. What is the nurse checking for?
options: The hospital's policy forms, signed by the client
The client's hemoglobin and platelet count
The client's history and physical examination
questions.rationale:
H&P is the history and physical, the provider's record of the client's health history and examination.

Hemoglobin and platelets are lab results, and height and pulse are measurements; neither is the H&P. Signed forms are consents, recorded separately.

Takeaway: H&P: history and physical.

questions.stem: A nurse is reading a client's health history. For each abbreviation, click to specify the condition the nurse should recognize.
columns: A clot in a deep vein, often in the leg
A clot that has traveled to the lungs
Heart muscle damaged by a blocked artery
Breathing that stops and starts during sleep
questions.rationale:
The abbreviations stand for PE, pulmonary embolism (a clot that has traveled to the lungs); OSA, obstructive sleep apnea; DVT, deep vein thrombosis (a clot in a deep vein, often in the leg); PNA, pneumonia; and MI, myocardial infarction.

Mixing up DVT and PE is a common mistake: a DVT is a clot in a vein, and a PE is a clot that has broken off and reached the lungs.

Takeaway: DVT in the leg, PE in the lungs, MI in the heart, PNA in the lungs' air spaces, OSA in sleep.

questions.stem: A client's history lists HTN, CKD, and BPH. Which of the following conditions should the nurse identify?
options: A blood clot in a leg
questions.rationale:
HTN is hypertension, high blood pressure; CKD is chronic kidney disease, long-term kidney damage; and BPH is an enlarged prostate.

Heart failure is HF, a clot in a leg is a DVT, and an underactive thyroid is hypothyroidism; none of them is in the history.

Takeaway: HTN high blood pressure, CKD chronic kidney disease, BPH enlarged prostate.

questions.stem: A client's care plan reads “No BP or blood draws, LUE.” Which action should the nurse take to check the client's blood pressure?
options: Ask the client which arm is less sore today
Use the left arm, with a smaller cuff
Skip the blood pressure for this shift
questions.rationale:
LUE is the left upper extremity, the left arm, so the blood pressure is taken on the right arm.

The left arm is the one the plan protects, whatever the cuff. Skipping it isn't needed, since the other arm can be used, and asking the client lets comfort override a safety order.

Takeaway: RUE, LUE: right and left arm; RLE, LLE: right and left leg.

questions.stem: A client's order reads “O2 2 L/min by nasal cannula, titrate to keep SpO2 92% or higher.” Which finding should the nurse act on?
options: RR 18/min while talking with a visitor
SpO2 89% after walking to the bathroom
AP 76/min and regular at the bedside
SpO2 95% while resting in bed after lunch
questions.rationale:
SpO2 is the oxygen saturation, and the order sets its goal at 92% or higher. 89% is below the goal, so the nurse titrates the O2 as ordered and rechecks.

95% meets the goal. RR 18 (respiratory rate) and AP 76 (apical pulse) are within normal limits.

Takeaway: SpO2 oxygen saturation, O2 oxygen, RR respiratory rate, AP apical pulse.

questions.stem: A client has a prescription for “Metoprolol 25 mg PO bid. Hold if AP below 60/min.” Which action should the nurse take before giving a dose?
options: Count the respirations for a full minute
Count the radial pulse for 30 seconds and double it
Listen at the apex of the heart for a full minute
Take the blood pressure on the right arm
questions.rationale:
AP is the apical pulse, heard with a stethoscope at the apex of the heart, counted for a full minute when a dose depends on it.

The radial pulse is felt at the wrist, not the apex. The blood pressure and the respirations (RR) aren't what the order names.

Takeaway: AP: apical pulse, listened to at the heart's apex.

questions.stem: A client has a prescription for “Ibuprofen 400 mg PO q6h PRN pain c̄ food.” Which instruction should the nurse give?
options: Take it an hour after you finish eating
Take it on an empty stomach
questions.rationale:
c̄ (c with a line over it) means with: take it with food.

An empty stomach is the opposite. Before meals is ac, and after is p̄ or pc.

Takeaway: a̅ before, p̄ after, c̄ with.

questions.stem: A client has a prescription for “Melatonin 3 mg PO hs.” When should the nurse give this medication?
options: Each hour until the client falls asleep
At half strength, mixed with water
questions.rationale:
hs is the hour of sleep: bedtime.

Half strength is a known misreading of hs, which is why some facilities write out “at bedtime.” Each hour mixes up hs with h, and the morning is qam.

Takeaway: hs: at bedtime. When in doubt, clarify.

questions.stem: During an admission interview, a client says, “I don't take any prescription medicines, just some OTC pain relievers.” Which response should the nurse make?
options: “Those don't need to go on your medication list.”
“Which ones do you take, and how often?”
“You'll need to stop taking them while you're here.”
“Over-the-counter medicines are safe with any prescription.”
questions.rationale:
OTC means over the counter, bought without a prescription. OTC medicines can interact with prescribed ones, so the nurse asks which ones, and how often, and adds them to the list.

Leaving them off the list hides possible interactions. Stopping them is the provider's decision, made with the full list. Safe with any prescription isn't true: OTC pain relievers can interact with prescribed drugs.

Takeaway: OTC: over the counter. Still medications: list them.

questions.stem: A client has a prescription for “Enoxaparin 40 mg subcut q24h.” The first dose was given Monday at 0900. When is the next dose due?
questions.rationale:
q24h means every 24 hours, once a day: the next dose is Tuesday at 0900.

Monday at 2100 would be q12h. Tuesday at 2100 is 36 hours later, and Wednesday is 48 hours later.

Takeaway: q24h: every 24 hours, the same time each day.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's medication orders. For each order, click to specify how many doses the nurse should give in 24 hours.
questions.rationale:
tid is 3 a day, bid 2, q6h every 6 hours (24 ÷ 6 = 4), q24h 1, q12h every 12 hours (2), and qid 4.

Reading q6h as 6 doses a day is a mistake: q6h is the time between doses, so it's 24 ÷ 6 = 4 doses.

Takeaway: bid 2, tid 3, qid 4; for qXh, divide 24 by X.

questions.stem: A client's order reads “Turn q2h.” The nurse turned the client at 2300 and again at 0045, after changing the bed. When is the next turn due?
questions.rationale:
q2h means every 2 hours from the last turn. The last turn was at 0045, so the next is due at 0245.

0100 counts from 2300 and ignores the turn at 0045. 0300 keeps to even hours, which isn't what q2h means, and 0445 is 4 hours later.

Takeaway: qXh counts from the last time it was done.

questions.stem: A client's order reads “NPO except meds.” It's 0800, and the client has scheduled oral medications. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give the medications with the breakfast tray
Hold the oral medications until the client can eat
Give the medications with a full glass of water
Give the medications with a small sip of water
questions.rationale:
NPO is nothing by mouth, but except meds allows the oral medications, with only a small sip of water to swallow them.

Holding them ignores the exception. A full glass of water and breakfast break the NPO order.

Takeaway: NPO except meds: medications with a sip, nothing else.

questions.stem: A nurse reads this entry in a client's record: “A&O x3. LLE cast. NKDA. Ambulate ad lib with crutches.” Which statements in the hand-off report are accurate?
options: The client knows who they are, where they are, and the time
The client has a cast on the left arm
The client has a cast on the left leg
The client has no known drug allergies
The client has no allergies of any kind
The client may walk with crutches as much as they like
questions.rationale:
A&O x3 is alert and oriented to person, place, and time; LLE is the left lower extremity, the left leg; NKDA is no known drug allergies; and ad lib is as much as desired.

The left arm would be LUE. No allergies of any kind would be NKA: NKDA rules out drug allergies only, so a food or latex allergy is still possible.

Takeaway: NKDA: no drug allergies; NKA: no allergies at all. LLE: left leg.

questions.stem: A nurse's calculation for an oral liquid comes to {v} mL. Using the class's rounding rules, how many milliliters should the nurse prepare?
questions.rationale:
The class's rule: an amount over 1 mL is rounded to the tenth. {v} rounds to a tenths place of 0, and a whole number is written without a trailing zero: {answer} mL.

Writing the zero after the decimal point is a mistake: a missed decimal point turns it into a dose 10 times too big. Leaving {v} unrounded breaks the rule.

Takeaway: Over 1 mL: round to the tenth, then drop a trailing zero.

questions.stem: A nurse's calculation for an injection comes to {v} mL. Which amount and syringe should the nurse use?
questions.rationale:
The class's rule: an amount under 1 mL is rounded to the hundredth, with a leading zero, and measured in a 1-mL (tuberculin) syringe: {=round(v, 2)} mL.

{=round(v, 1)} mL rounds to the tenth, the rule for amounts over 1 mL. A 3-mL syringe can't measure hundredths, and .{=round(v * 100)} mL leaves out the leading zero.

Takeaway: Under 1 mL: the hundredth, a leading zero, and a 1-mL syringe.

questions.stem: A nurse sees “Give 5.0 mL” on a classmate's medication worksheet. Which error could this cause?
options: No error, since 5.0 mL and 5 mL are the same amount
Someone could read it as 0.5 mL and underdose the client
Someone could miss the decimal point and give 50 mL
Someone could give 5 mg instead of 5 mL
questions.rationale:
A trailing zero hides the decimal point: if it's missed, 5.0 reads as 50, a dose 10 times too big.

0.5 mL is the risk of a missing leading zero (.5), not a trailing one. The unit isn't changed by the zero, and the amounts are the same only if the decimal point is seen.

Takeaway: No trailing zeros: 5, not 5.0.

questions.stem: A client drank 1/3 of a {c}-mL bottle of a nutrition shake at breakfast, at lunch, and at dinner. How many milliliters should the nurse record for the three meals?
questions.rationale:
Three thirds of the bottle is the whole bottle: {c} mL. The class's rule is to round at the end, not at each step.

{=round(c / 3) * 3} mL rounds each meal's {=round(c / 3, 2)} mL before adding, which builds up an error. {=round(c / 3)} mL is one meal only, and {=c * 3} mL counts three whole bottles.

Takeaway: Round once, at the end of the problem.

questions.stem: A nurse is checking a classmate's calculations. For each result, click to specify how the nurse should round it.
columns: To the hundredth, with a leading zero
questions.rationale:
Under 1 mL, round to the hundredth with a leading zero (0.376 becomes 0.38, and 0.843 becomes 0.84). Over 1 mL, round to the tenth (1.57 becomes 1.6, and 2.46 becomes 2.5). Drops and units can't be divided, so they're rounded to a whole number (31.25 gtt becomes 31, and 2,537.5 units becomes 2,538).

Rounding every result the same way is a mistake: the rule depends on the amount and on what can be measured.

Takeaway: Under 1 mL: hundredth. Over 1 mL: tenth. Drops and units: whole number.

questions.stem: A client's temperature is {f} °F. Which temperature in degrees Celsius should the nurse document?
questions.rationale:
°C = (°F − 32) × 5/9. First subtract: {f} − 32 = {=round(f - 32, 1)}. Then multiply by 5/9: {=round((f - 32) * 5 / 9, 2)}, which rounds to {answer} °C.

Multiplying before subtracting 32 is a mistake: subtract first, then multiply.

Takeaway: °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9; °F = °C × 9/5 + 32.

questions.stem: A client takes {t} of a liquid antacid {n}. How many milliliters should the nurse expect the client to take in a day?
questions.rationale:
1 Tbsp = 15 mL, so one dose is {t} × 15 = {=t * 15} mL. Given {n}, that's {=t * 15} × {=n} = {answer} mL a day.

Using 5 mL for each tablespoon is a mistake: 5 mL is a teaspoon. Stopping at one dose leaves out the daily total.

Takeaway: 1 tsp = 5 mL, 1 Tbsp = 15 mL; bid 2, tid 3, qid 4 doses.

questions.stem: A client drank {oz} oz of fluids today. How many liters should the nurse document?
questions.rationale:
First to mL: {oz} × 30 = {=oz * 30} mL. Then to L: {=oz * 30} ÷ 1,000 = {answer} L.

Dividing the ounces by 1,000 skips a step: ounces become mL first, then liters.

Takeaway: oz × 30 = mL; mL ÷ 1,000 = L.

questions.stem: A client's IV bag held {l} of fluid. At the end of the shift, {left} mL remain in the bag. How many milliliters have infused?
questions.rationale:
{l} = {=l * 1000} mL (× 1,000). What infused is what's gone: {=l * 1000} − {left} = {answer} mL.

Subtracting the mL from the liters without converting is a mistake: change the liters to mL first.

Takeaway: L × 1,000 = mL; infused = start − left.

questions.stem: A client has a prescription for “Acetaminophen {d} mg PO q6h.” How many grams should the nurse expect the client to receive in 24 hours?
questions.rationale:
q6h is every 6 hours: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 doses. {d} × 4 = {=d * 4} mg, and mg ÷ 1,000 = g: {=d * 4 / 1000} g.

{=d * 6 / 1000} g reads q6h as 6 doses. {=d / 1000} g is one dose, and {=d * 4} g forgets to change mg to g.

Takeaway: Doses a day first, then mg ÷ 1,000 = g.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure has gained {g} kg since yesterday. How many pounds should the nurse report?
questions.rationale:
1 kg = 2.2 lb, so multiply: {g} × 2.2 = {=round(g * 2.2, 2)}, which rounds to {answer} lb.

Dividing by 2.2 is a mistake: pounds are the smaller unit, so the number gets bigger.

Takeaway: kg to lb: × 2.2; lb to kg: ÷ 2.2.

questions.stem: A provider prescribes {vol} mL of 0.9% sodium chloride IV over {h} hours. At how many mL/hr should the nurse set the pump?
questions.rationale:
Rate = volume ÷ hours: {vol} ÷ {h} = {=round(vol / h, 2)}, which rounds to {answer} mL/hr.

Multiplying the volume by the hours is a mistake: a rate is mL for each hour, so divide.

Takeaway: mL/hr = total mL ÷ hours.

questions.stem: An IV antibiotic of {vol} mL is to infuse over {m} minutes. At how many mL/hr should the nurse set the pump?
questions.rationale:
The pump runs in mL per hour, so change the minutes to hours: {m} ÷ 60. Then {vol} ÷ ({m} ÷ 60) = {vol} × 60 ÷ {m} = {=round(vol * 60 / m)} mL/hr.

{=round(vol / m, 2)} is mL per minute, not per hour. {=round(vol * m / 60)} turns the time the wrong way, and {vol} mL/hr gives the whole bag in an hour.

Takeaway: Minutes to hours first: mL/hr = mL × 60 ÷ minutes.

questions.stem: A {vol}-mL bag of IV fluid is infusing at {r} mL/hr. How many hours should the nurse expect the infusion to take?
questions.rationale:
Time = volume ÷ rate: {vol} ÷ {r} = {=round(vol / r, 2)}, which rounds to {answer} hours.

Multiplying the volume by the rate is a mistake: divide the volume by the mL each hour.

Takeaway: Hours = mL ÷ mL/hr.

questions.stem: A newborn weighs {lb} lb {oz} oz. Which weight in kilograms should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
A pound has 16 ounces, so {oz} oz = {=oz / 16} lb, and the newborn weighs {=lb + oz / 16} lb. Then ÷ 2.2: {=round((lb + oz / 16) / 2.2, 1)} kg.

{=round((lb + oz / 10) / 2.2, 1)} kg treats the ounces as a decimal, as if a pound had 10 ounces. {=round(lb / 2.2, 1)} kg leaves out the ounces, and {=round((lb + oz / 16) * 2.2, 1)} kg multiplies instead of dividing.

Takeaway: Ounces ÷ 16 = pounds; then pounds ÷ 2.2 = kg.

questions.stem: A parent will give a child {ml} mL of a liquid medicine at home with a measuring teaspoon. How many teaspoons should the nurse teach the parent to give?
questions.rationale:
1 tsp = 5 mL, so divide: {ml} ÷ 5 = {=ml / 5} tsp.

{=round(ml / 15, 2)} tsp uses 15 mL, which is a tablespoon, and {=round(ml / 30, 2)} tsp uses 30 mL, an ounce. {=ml * 5} tsp multiplies instead of dividing.

Takeaway: 1 tsp = 5 mL; 1 Tbsp = 15 mL; 1 oz = 30 mL.

questions.stem: An IV medication of {vol} mL is infusing at {r} mL/hr. How many minutes should the nurse expect the infusion to take?
questions.rationale:
Hours first: {vol} ÷ {r} = {=round(vol / r, 4)} hours. Then × 60: {answer} minutes.

Stopping at {=round(vol / r, 4)} is a mistake: that's the time in hours, and the question asks for minutes.

Takeaway: Hours = mL ÷ mL/hr; minutes = hours × 60.

questions.stem: A client receives a tube feeding at {r} mL/hr for {h} hours, with a {f}-mL water flush every 4 hours. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record for the {h} hours?
questions.rationale:
Feeding: {r} × {h} = {=r * h} mL. Flushes: {h} hours ÷ 4 = {=h / 4} flushes × {f} = {=h / 4 * f} mL. Total: {answer} mL.

Leaving out the flushes is a mistake: water given through the tube is intake too.

Takeaway: Tube feedings and flushes both count as intake.

questions.stem: During an 8-hour shift, a client's IV pump ran at {r} mL/hr, and the client also received {n} of {p} mL each. How many milliliters of IV intake should the nurse record for the shift?
questions.rationale:
Pump: {r} × 8 = {=r * 8} mL. Antibiotics: {n} × {p} = {=n * p} mL. Total: {answer} mL.

Leaving out the IV antibiotics is a mistake: every IV fluid counts toward intake.

Takeaway: IV intake = rate × hours + every other IV fluid given.

questions.stem: During a shift, a client drank {a} oz of water and {b} oz of juice, and {iv} mL of IV fluid infused. Which amount should the nurse record as the client's oral intake?
questions.rationale:
Oral intake is what the client took by mouth: ({a} + {b}) × 30 = {=(a + b) * 30} mL. The IV fluid counts in the total intake, not the oral intake.

{=(a + b) * 30 + iv} mL adds the IV fluid, which makes it the total intake. {=a * 30} mL leaves out the juice, and {=(a + b) * 15} mL uses 15 mL an ounce, a tablespoon's worth.

Takeaway: Oral intake: by mouth only. Total intake: oral plus IV and tube feedings.

questions.stem: A client drank 2/3 of a {oz}-oz cup of tea and half of a {m}-mL carton of milk. How many milliliters should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Tea: {oz} × 30 = {=oz * 30} mL, and 2/3 of it is {=oz * 20} mL. Milk: half of {m} = {=m / 2} mL. Total: {answer} mL.

Recording the full cup and carton is a mistake: count only what the client drank.

Takeaway: Convert, take the part drunk, then add.

questions.stem: A client was given a {g}-oz glass of milk and a 240-mL carton of juice. The client finished the juice, and {left} oz of milk remain in the glass. How many milliliters should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Milk drunk: {g} − {left} = {=g - left} oz × 30 = {=(g - left) * 30} mL. Juice: 240 mL. Total: {answer} mL.

Recording the milk that's left is a mistake: intake is what the client drank, the glass minus what remains.

Takeaway: Intake = what was served − what's left.

questions.stem: For a client's 24-hour intake, the day shift recorded {d} mL and the evening shift {e} mL. On the night shift, the client drank {w} oz of water and ate {c} mL of ice chips. How many milliliters should the nurse record as the 24-hour intake?
questions.rationale:
Night shift: water {w} × 30 = {=w * 30} mL, and ice chips {c} ÷ 2 = {=c / 2} mL. 24 hours: {d} + {e} + {=w * 30} + {=c / 2} = {answer} mL.

Counting the ice chips at full volume is a mistake: they count as half, even inside a 24-hour total.

Takeaway: Add every shift's total; halve the ice chips.

questions.stem: A client has a fluid restriction of {lim} mL a day: half for the day shift, a third for the evening shift, and the rest for the night shift. How many milliliters should the nurse allow on the night shift?
questions.rationale:
Day: {lim} ÷ 2 = {=lim / 2} mL. Evening: {lim} ÷ 3 = {=lim / 3} mL. Night gets the rest: {lim} − {=lim / 2} − {=lim / 3} = {answer} mL.

Giving the night shift a third is a mistake: half plus a third leaves a sixth for nights.

Takeaway: A restriction's shares add up to the whole: 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6.

questions.stem: A client on intake and output has chicken broth, gelatin, a turkey sandwich, ice cream, mashed potatoes, and a banana for lunch. Which items should the nurse count as fluid intake?
questions.rationale:
Fluids are anything liquid at room temperature: broth, gelatin, and ice cream, which melts.

A sandwich, mashed potatoes, and a banana are solid foods, which aren't recorded as intake, though they contain some water.

Takeaway: Liquid at room temperature counts: broth, gelatin, ice cream, popsicles.

questions.stem: A nurse is totaling a client's intake and output. For each item, click to specify how the nurse should record it.
rows: A saline flush through the IV
questions.rationale:
Ice chips count as half their volume. Gelatin and a saline flush through the IV count in full (the flush toward the total intake). Vomit and urine are output. Toast is solid food, so it isn't recorded.

Halving the gelatin is a mistake: only ice chips are halved, since they're mostly air spaces. Subtracting the vomit from the intake is a mistake too: it's recorded as output.

Takeaway: Ice chips: half. Liquids, gelatin, flushes: full. Vomit, urine: output. Solids: not recorded.

questions.stem: At lunch, a client drank {a} oz of coffee and {b} oz of juice and ate half of a {s}-mL bowl of soup. Which intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Coffee and juice: ({a} + {b}) × 30 = {=(a + b) * 30} mL. Soup: half of {s} = {=s / 2} mL. Total: {=(a + b) * 30 + s / 2} mL.

{=(a + b) * 30 + s} mL counts the whole bowl of soup. {=(a + b) * 15 + s / 2} mL uses 15 mL an ounce, a tablespoon's worth, and {=(a + b) * 30} mL leaves out the soup, which is a liquid and counts.

Takeaway: 1 oz = 30 mL; count only the part eaten.

questions.stem: A client drank {n} cups of coffee from 6-oz cups and {w} mL of water. How many milliliters should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Each cup holds 6 oz × 30 = 180 mL, so {n} cups = {=n * 180} mL. Add the water: {answer} mL.

Using 240 mL for each cup is a mistake here: 240 mL is a standard 8-oz cup, and these cups hold 6 oz.

Takeaway: Use the container's real size: oz × 30 = mL.

questions.stem: A client's IV ran at {r} mL/hr from 0700 to 1500, except for {off} while the client was in radiology. How many milliliters of IV intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
0700 to 1500 is 8 hours; minus the time it was off, it ran {=8 - off} hours: {r} × {=8 - off} = {answer} mL.

Multiplying the rate by all 8 hours is a mistake: the IV wasn't running while it was off.

Takeaway: IV intake = rate × the hours it actually ran.

questions.stem: A client ate {part} of a {oz}-oz cup of ice chips. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
The cup holds {oz} × 30 = {=oz * 30} mL. The client ate {part} of it, {=oz * 30 * part} mL of ice chips, which count as half: {answer} mL.

Halving the cup and forgetting the part eaten is a mistake: find what was eaten, then halve it.

Takeaway: Ounces to mL, the part eaten, then half for ice.

questions.stem: A client in labor eats about {c} mL of ice chips each hour. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record for {h} hours?
questions.rationale:
{c} × {h} = {=c * h} mL of ice chips, which count as half: {answer} mL.

Recording the full {=c * h} mL is a mistake: ice chips melt down to about half their volume.

Takeaway: Total the ice chips, then halve them.

questions.stem: During a shift, a client ate {c} mL of ice chips and drank {j} oz of juice, and {iv} mL of IV fluid infused. How many milliliters should the nurse record as the client's oral intake?
questions.rationale:
Oral intake is by mouth only: ice chips {c} ÷ 2 = {=c / 2} mL, and juice {j} × 30 = {=j * 30} mL, for {answer} mL. The IV fluid counts in the total intake, not the oral intake.

Adding the {iv} mL of IV fluid is a mistake here: it isn't taken by mouth.

Takeaway: Oral intake: halve the ice chips, add the drinks, leave out the IV.

questions.stem: During an 8-hour shift, a client ate {c} mL of ice chips, and an IV infused at {r} mL/hr. Which total intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Ice chips: {c} ÷ 2 = {=c / 2} mL. IV: {r} × 8 = {=r * 8} mL. Total intake: {=c / 2 + r * 8} mL.

{=c + r * 8} mL counts the ice chips at full volume. {=c / 2 + r} mL counts the IV for only 1 hour, and {=c / 2} mL is the oral intake alone.

Takeaway: Total intake: oral (ice chips halved) plus IV.

questions.stem: During a shift, a client ate {n} full cups of ice chips and half of one more. Each cup holds {cup} mL. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
{n} cups and a half = {=n + 0.5} cups × {cup} = {=(n + 0.5) * cup} mL of ice chips, which count as half: {answer} mL.

Halving only the last half cup is a mistake: every cup of ice chips counts as half.

Takeaway: Add up all the ice chips, then halve the total.

questions.stem: A client ate {c} mL of ice chips, {g} mL of gelatin, and a slice of toast. Which intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Ice chips count as half: {c} ÷ 2 = {=c / 2} mL. Gelatin is liquid at room temperature, so it counts in full: {g} mL. Toast is solid food. Total: {=c / 2 + g} mL.

{=c / 2 + g / 2} mL halves the gelatin too, but only ice chips are halved. {=c + g} mL counts the ice chips in full, and {=c / 2} mL leaves out the gelatin.

Takeaway: Only ice chips are halved; gelatin counts in full; solids aren't recorded.

questions.stem: A client has a fluid restriction of {lim} mL a day and has had {had} mL so far today. The client asks for ice chips. How many milliliters of ice chips can the client have and stay within the restriction?
questions.rationale:
The client has {lim} − {had} = {=lim - had} mL of fluid left. Ice chips count as half their volume, so the client can have twice that in ice chips: {=lim - had} × 2 = {answer} mL.

Stopping at {=lim - had} mL is a mistake: that's the fluid left, and ice chips only count as half of it.

Takeaway: Fluid left × 2 = the ice chips allowed.

questions.stem: During a shift, a client ate {n} cups of ice chips. Each cup holds 6 oz. Which intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Each cup holds 6 × 30 = 180 mL of ice chips, which count as half: 90 mL a cup. {n} cups: {=n * 90} mL.

{=n * 180} mL counts the ice chips at full volume. {=n * 120} mL uses an 8-oz (240-mL) cup, and {=n * 45} mL uses 15 mL an ounce.

Takeaway: Container size × 30, then half for ice.

questions.stem: A client ate {c} mL of ice chips and a {p}-mL fruit popsicle. Which intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Ice chips are half air, so they count as half: {c} ÷ 2 = {=c / 2} mL. A popsicle is frozen liquid with no air spaces, so it counts in full: {p} mL. Total: {=c / 2 + p} mL.

{=(c + p) / 2} mL halves the popsicle too. {=c + p} mL counts the ice chips at full volume, and {=c / 2} mL leaves out the popsicle.

Takeaway: Halve ice chips only; popsicles, ice cream, and gelatin count in full.

questions.stem: A {oz}-oz cup was filled with ice chips at 0700 and refilled at 1100. By 1500, the client had eaten the first cup and all but {left} of the second. How many milliliters of intake should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Eaten: the first cup ({oz} oz) and {=1 - left} of the second ({=oz * (1 - left)} oz), for {=oz + oz * (1 - left)} oz × 30 = {=(oz + oz * (1 - left)) * 30} mL of ice chips, which count as half: {answer} mL.

Counting both cups in full is a mistake: part of the second wasn't eaten, and all of it is ice.

Takeaway: Add what was eaten from every cup, convert, then halve.

questions.stem: A nurse is checking the meanings a new nurse wrote next to abbreviations in her notes. For each one, click to specify whether the meaning is correct or incorrect.
questions.rationale:
tid is three times a day (bid twice, qid four times). pc is after meals; before meals is ac. OU is both eyes; the left eye is OS, and the right is OD. NPO is nothing by mouth. NKDA is no known drug allergies, not dietary. DVT is deep vein thrombosis, a clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg.

Mixing up ac and pc changes when a dose is given with meals, and mixing up OU, OD, and OS puts eye drops in the wrong eye, so these are worth checking every time.

Takeaway: tid three times a day, pc after meals (ac before), OU both eyes (OD right, OS left), NPO nothing by mouth, NKDA no known drug allergies, DVT deep vein thrombosis.

questions.stem: A nurse is checking a student's calculations. For each entry, click to specify whether it's correct or incorrect.
rows: 1 1/2 cups of juice = 360 mL of intake
A volume of 2.5 mL, recorded as “2.50 mL”
questions.rationale:
Grams to milligrams: × 1,000, so 0.5 g = 500 mg. Pounds to kilograms: ÷ 2.2, so 44 lb = 20 kg. One teaspoon is 5 mL, so 2 tsp = 10 mL, not 15 (15 mL is 1 tablespoon). Celsius to Fahrenheit: × 9/5 + 32, so 38 °C = 68.4 + 32 = 100.4 °F. One cup is 8 oz, or 240 mL, so 1 1/2 cups = 360 mL. And “2.50 mL” has a trailing zero, which isn't allowed: it's written 2.5 mL.

The 15 mL is a tablespoon's volume, so it's easy to give a teaspoon the wrong one; check which spoon the order names.

Takeaway: g to mg: × 1,000. lb to kg: ÷ 2.2. 1 tsp = 5 mL, 1 Tbsp = 15 mL. °F = °C × 9/5 + 32. 1 cup = 240 mL. No trailing zeros.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how volumes were rounded and written in a client's record. For each entry, click to specify whether it follows the rules or breaks one.
rows: A dose of 0.456 mL, written as 0.46 mL
A dose of 0.75 mL, written as .75 mL
A dose of 3 mL, written as 3.0 mL
A dose of 1.46 mL, written as 1.5 mL
8 oz of milk and 4 oz of soup, recorded as 360 mL of intake
A dose of 2.25 mL, written as 2.2 mL
questions.rationale:
Under 1 mL, round to the hundredth and write a leading zero: 0.456 becomes 0.46 mL, and .75 must be written 0.75 mL. A trailing zero is never written: 3 mL, not 3.0. Over 1 mL, round to the tenth, and 5 or more rounds up: 1.46 becomes 1.5 mL, and 2.25 becomes 2.3 mL, not 2.2. Intake: 8 + 4 = 12 oz, and 12 × 30 = 360 mL.

The 2.2 drops the 5 instead of rounding it up, which underdoses. And “.75” is the right amount but the wrong way to write it: a missing leading zero can be misread as 75.

Takeaway: Under 1 mL: the hundredth, with a leading zero. Over 1 mL: the tenth, 5 or more rounding up. Never a trailing zero. 1 oz = 30 mL.
